About this citation

Line numbering differs between the Weimar edition and modern reading texts, so the archive records the scene; a scholarly citation would give the line number in a named edition.

Exact wording

English (as recorded here)
“Two souls, alas, are dwelling in my breast.”
German
“Zwei Seelen wohnen, ach! in meiner Brust.”

Faust I, “Before the City Gate.” Faust speaks of two souls; English “alas” for ach is conventional.

Forms in circulation that differ

  • “Two souls, alas, are dwelling in my breast.”
  • “Two souls dwell, alas, in my breast.”

Attribution notes

Goethe, Faust I. Spoken by Faust about the pull between earthly desire and ascent to higher worlds — not a generic confession of indecision. Detaching it from Faust's speech makes it a personality type instead of a dramatic beat.

About Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

Johann Wolfgang von Goethe (1749–1832) was Germany’s preeminent writer whose scientific and reflective works engage morphology, color, and the formation of life and character.

Interpretation

Goethe gives this to Faust at a moment of paralysis, and it describes a divided will rather than a moral failing. One impulse reaches beyond the limits of a human life; the other clings to what can be secured. Faust's tragedy is not that he has two souls but that the conflict prevents either from governing, so he neither commits nor rests. The line is diagnostic — Goethe is showing what the condition costs before offering any resolution.

Why it matters

It names a recognisable state: the exhaustion comes less from wanting two things than from the inability to choose, which turns either option into a loss.

Questions readers arrive with

What is the source of the quotation “Two souls, alas, are dwelling in my breast.”?

“Two souls, alas, are dwelling in my breast.” comes from Faust, Part One (1808), attributed to Johann Wolfgang von Goethe.

What does Johann Wolfgang von Goethe mean by self?

To ask about the self is to ask what persists through experience, what can be known from the first-person point of view, and how character is formed. Some traditions treat the self as a substantial soul; others as a stream of experience, a social role, or a practical center of agency. This passage enters that discussion through self.

Is the wording of this Johann Wolfgang von Goethe quotation commonly changed?

The wording recorded here is “Two souls, alas, are dwelling in my breast.” Forms in circulation that differ: Two souls, alas, are dwelling in my breast. / Two souls dwell, alas, in my breast. The German reads “Zwei Seelen wohnen, ach! in meiner Brust.”

Is this quotation attributed correctly?

Goethe, Faust I. Spoken by Faust about the pull between earthly desire and ascent to higher worlds — not a generic confession of indecision. Detaching it from Faust's speech makes it a personality type instead of a dramatic beat.
